https://telex.hu/karakter/kultura/2026/0.text: Menü Kereső Meghalt Kardos Sándor Kossuth-díjas operatőr és fotográfus Kultúra Kardos Sándor 2022-ben – Fotó: Cseke Csilla / MTI Krász Zsombor 82 éves korában meghalt Kardos Sándor Kossuth- és Balázs Béla-díjas operatőr, rendező és fotográfus – tudatta az MTI-vel a Magyar Művészeti Akadémia. Az akadémia rendes tagja volt, 2022-ben a Nemzet Művészének választották . Kardos Sándor 1944-ben született Budapesten. 1969-ben végezte el az ELTE magyar-népművelés szakát, majd 1973-ban operatőrként szerzett diplomát a Színház- és Filmművészeti Főiskolán. 1972-től a MAFILM-nél volt segédoperatőr, 1979-től pedig a Magyar Televízió operatőre és rendezője lett. Élete során több mint harminc játékfilmet és száznál is több tévéfilmet, kisjátékfilmet fényképezett. Olyan filmek egyedi fényképezése fűződik a nevéhez, mint A kis Valentinó, az Álombrigád, A tanítványok és az Eldorádó. Filmrendezőként főként kísérleti filmeket készített, így például a Hymnus-t, a Résfilmet és az Átváltozást. Kardos Sándor privátfotó-gyűjteménye, a Hórusz Archívum Magyarország legnagyobb magánkollekciója. Korábban a Telexen is rendszeresen mutattunk be a kollekció képeiből. Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! Legfontosabb Friss hírek

https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/28/ukra.text: Ukrainian forces have delivered around 4 tonnes of food to the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in the Kherson region by drone in one of the largest such operations of the war, as roughly 2,000 remaining residents face what international organisations have described as a worsening humanitarian catastrophe.Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022. No food has reached the city through regular channels since May of this year, according to ground reports.Meanwhile, Russian forces are blocking civilians from evacuating and actively obstructing drone deliveries.Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the Kherson regional military administration, said troops are shooting down food-carrying drones, confiscating or reselling supplies that reach the ground, and detaining residents found with humanitarian parcels.Soldiers are conducting house-to-house searches for dropped food, residents report.Ukrainian forces have been delivering aid by drone across the Dnipro since March, the regional administration said. The location and timing of individual operations are withheld for security reasons. Ukrainian troops hold positions on the right bank of the Dnipro, several kilometres from the city.Thousands in peril of deathThe regional military administration puts the population still in Oleshky at around 2,000, including nearly 50 children, down from 25,000 residents before Russia's all-out invasion in early 2022.The All-Ukrainian Council of Churches and Religious Organisations estimates more than 6,000 people remain in the city and surrounding area, including around 200 children.Ukrainian officials say anyone suspected of contact with Ukrainian authorities or armed forces faces immediate execution.Conditions in the city have deteriorated sharply since the destruction of the Kakhovka hydroelectric dam in June 2023, which flooded large parts of the region, destroyed hundreds of homes and blocked wells and sewage systems. At least 200 to 300 people died in Oleshky in the flooding alone.Residents now rely primarily on their own gardens for food, face chronic medicine shortages and move between abandoned buildings to avoid drone raids and looting by Russian troops, according to reports from the city."People are lying on the roads, rotting, unburied. Today in the basement of the hospital, the very one that has had no electricity for four years now, there are more than 100 corpses," Tetyana Hasanenko, an employee of the Oleshky city military administration, told ABC News.The 34th Separate Marine Brigade "Borysfen," involved in the drone deliveries, published footage from the city in April that it described as showing a settlement Russian forces had "turned into a ghost town"."People are forced to eat grass and weeds to survive. The roads are mined, it is almost impossible to get out safely, and shelling and drone attacks continue all around," Musician Artem Pivovarov said."There are reports that the bodies of those killed remain on the streets for months, there is no one to collect them."Evacuation plan obstructed by MoscowKyiv has drawn up a humanitarian evacuation plan that the International Committee of the Red Cross is prepared to join.Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said Russia has not confirmed its readiness to allow the mission to proceed. Without agreed access, volunteers cannot enter the city on their own.Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has called on international organisations to secure humanitarian access."Russia is deliberately provoking a humanitarian catastrophe in the occupied part of the Kherson region. It is blocking access to food and medicine, obstructing the delivery of humanitarian aid and the evacuation of civilians, while Russian FPV drones hunt people in the streets," Sybiha said.The UN mission in Ukraine described the situation in Oleshky as "desperate" in June, saying thousands of civilians faced "a serious threat to their lives, a lack of food and no access to medical care."Michael O'Flaherty, the Council of Europe's Commissioner for Human Rights, said he was "alarmed by the rapidly worsening humanitarian crisis"."Civilians, including children, are trapped without sufficient food, medicines, medical care, running water or electricity," O'Flaherty said in a statement."Reports indicate that they face a high risk of death."O'Flaherty reminded Russia of its legal obligations: under international humanitarian law, the occupying power must ensure the population has access to food and medicines.Ukrainian tennis player Oleksandra Oliinykova, ranked world number 47, drew public attention to the city on social media: "Please, google Oleshky. It is a town that is currently under temporary occupation. There is a humanitarian catastrophe there."Ukrainian supporters displayed a banner reading "Save Oleshky" during a recent Hungary-Ukraine football match.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov acknowledged the situation in Oleshky was "indeed critical" but blamed the "Kyiv regime" for blocking deliveries.Oleshky is not the only Ukrainian settlement rendered uninhabitable under Russian occupation or bombardment since February 2022.Mariupol, a port city of around 425,000 people, was razed in a weeks-long Russian siege in spring 2022, while Bakhmut and Avdiivka in the Donetsk region were almost entirely destroyed before falling to Russian forces in 2023 and 2024, respectively.Towns including Volnovakha, Rubizhne and Maryinka have been reduced to rubble along the frontline. Ukrainian authorities estimate more than 210,000 buildings have been destroyed across the country since the full-scale invasion began.

Photograph: Sarah Wilson/AAP New South Wales NSW police commissioner made last-minute bid to hold closed-door hearings into Sydney anti-Herzog protest Police watchdog says Mal Lanyon’s timing in raising the issue was ‘regrettable’ and led to delays Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Penry Buckley and Jordyn Beazley Thu 8 Oct 2026 01.30 EDT Last modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 02.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The New South Wales police commissioner made a last-minute bid to hold hearings into Sydney’s anti-Herzog protest behind closed doors, delaying the inquiry, the police watchdog has revealed. The Law Enforcement Conduct Commission (Lecc) has said that its inquiry into the February protest at Sydney’s town hall, launched after widespread allegations of police brutality, would go ahead this month with a mix of public and private examinations, saying the timing of issues raised by police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, was “regrettable”. Lecc launched an investigation after the protest on 9 February, during which numerous protesters – and 10 officers – were injured, including demonstrators in their 70s and 80s. Viral video footage showed police punching multiple protesters, and grabbing Muslim worshippers while they undertook their sunset prayers. An ‘impossible’ situation or ‘unhinged’ police? Inside the chaos at Sydney’s anti-Herzog protest Read more Thirty people were charged in the months after the protest, but four have since had their charges dropped. More than 20 of those charged are due to face a joint hearing next July. In a decision made public on Thursday, the Lecc chief commissioner, Peter Johnson SC, revealed that legal representatives for Lanyon had indicated for the “first time” on 9 September that he wished to be heard on the issue of public and private examinations. The bid was made less than two weeks before the public hearings between September and November were due to start. Some hearings were also expected to be heard in private. “The timing of these issues being raised by the Commissioner of Police is more than regrettable given its impact on the orderly progress of the investigation, the preparation for examinations and the efficient and effective use of public resources by both the Commission and the NSWPF and the associated cost and disruption flowing from the delay,” Johnson said. Johnson said the start date of public hearings, 21 September, was subsequently delayed to “a date to be fixed” to allow a private hearing for submissions on the issue. 1:01 NSW police punch person multiple times during Sydney anti-Herzog protest – video Lawyers acting on behalf of Lanyon submitted that Lecc’s opening address and the examination of witnesses should occur in private and not be livestreamed. They argued that the Lecc Act does not have the power to hear “broad ranging open submissions” and said Lecc should not take the “unconventional approach of hearing opening submissions in public part way through an investigation that is already underway”. But Lecc argued that it does have the power to decide when public examinations are appropriate. The counsel assisting submitted that public examinations were necessary because “there was already significant information concerning the events of 9 February 2026 in the public domain, including footage of use of force by police” and that senior police officers had advanced in public an “official narrative of what took place”. “Public comments made by senior police increase the need for independent scrutiny,” the commissioner wrote. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The counsel assisting had pointed to specific features of the investigation as reason for why only private examinations were not appropriate. This included the “significant public concern” after the protest, including in parts of the Islamic community in Western Sydney. On Thursday, the watchdog said its inquiry into the protest would begin with a public address by counsel assisting on 19 October, followed by five weeks of private hearings. Lecc expects senior officers will then appear at public examinations. 2:00 Pepper spray and questionable police tactics: how a Sydney protest ended in chaos – video It said its Operation Makalu inquiry would analyse the use of OC spray, as well as the “improper use of arrest powers and the police use of force” at the protest. It will consider police planning ahead of the protest and “any opportunities for improvement in the policing of protests”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion In his decision, the commissioner determined that private examinations would be held on “issues of fact” while public examinations would be held to deal with systemic issues, but only after the private examinations have been held. In September, Palestinian Australian Eyad Shadid launched a civil case in the NSW district court , alleging he was assaulted, battered and falsely imprisoned by police near Sydney’s town hall. He alleged in his statement of claim that NSW police committed misfeasance in public office and subjected him to a malicious prosecution. In a statement, NSW Greens justice spokesperson, Sue Higginson, described the push to hold hearings in private as “an extraordinary attempt by the police to suppress the public examination of allegations of serious misconduct by uniformed police officers, and to prevent public scrutiny of the political decisions and command structures that led to police violence against protesters”. At a NSW parliamentary inquiry in May, Johnson said police had become “overly defensive” in response to requests for information in its investigations, describing the relationship between the agencies as “difficult”. He said the Lecc had received a record number of complaints, more than 800, as part of its investigation into the Herzog protest. In a statement following Johnson’s comments, NSW police said it “complied with the requirements of the LECC Act in a cooperative manner”. NSW police said in a statement it acknowledged the decision to hold private hearings and awaited the findings.
